nameStory: The "rattlesnake root" name comes from an old belief that these plants could cure rattlesnake bites, though there's no scientific evidence for this folk remedy. The "purple" part refers to the purplish stems and flower heads that distinguish this species from its white-flowered relatives.
description: Purple rattlesnake root is a tall, slender wildflower that can reach 3-6 feet in height, belonging to the diverse daisy family. Despite its name, the small drooping flower heads are more cream-colored than purple, but the stems and flower parts often have a distinctive purplish tinge. It's a graceful plant with deeply lobed leaves and an open, branching flower cluster that nods elegantly in wet meadows and along stream banks. This is one of our rarer wildflowers, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and slender with an open, branching top that creates an airy, delicate appearance unlike the dense clusters of many other wildflowers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, drooping, bell-shaped flower heads that hang downward on thin stalks, cream to pale yellow in color with purplish bracts underneath

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves that feel smooth to the touch, with the lower leaves much larger than the small upper ones, creating a distinctive tiered effect

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth stems with a noticeable purplish or reddish tinge, especially toward the top where the flowers branch out

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white seed heads that form after flowering, each seed topped with a parachute-like tuft that catches the slightest breeze

habitat: Look for purple rattlesnake root in consistently moist areas like streambanks, boggy meadows, wet prairies, and the edges of marshes. It prefers rich, organic soils that stay damp throughout the growing season. You'll often find it growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like wild mint, monkey flower, and various sedges.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as a rosette of deeply lobed basal leaves that are much more prominent than they'll be later in the season.
seasonality.summer: The tall flowering stem shoots up in mid to late summer, topped with the characteristic drooping, cream-colored flower heads that bloom from July through August.
seasonality.fall: After flowering, the plant produces fluffy white seed heads that disperse on autumn breezes, while the leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Purple rattlesnake root is so rare in New England that it's been documented fewer than a dozen times across all six states, making it one of our most elusive native wildflowers—spotting one is like finding botanical treasure!
confusionNotes: The drooping, bell-shaped flower heads and wet habitat preferences distinguish it from other rattlesnake roots, most of which prefer drier woodlands and have more upright flower clusters. Remember: if it's hanging its head in a wet spot, it's likely the purple species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the common name suggesting danger, rattlesnake roots are completely harmless plants that were actually considered medicinal by indigenous peoples and early settlers. The "glaucous white lettuce" alternate name reflects its relationship to lettuces and refers to the pale, waxy coating sometimes visible on the leaves.
compareHints: Purple rattlesnake root stands apart from its relatives by preferring wet habitats while most other rattlesnake roots grow in dry woods or clearings. Its drooping flower heads and purplish stems are distinctive—white rattlesnake root has upright white flowers in forests, while tall rattlesnake root forms dense upright clusters in woodland edges. The wet feet and nodding flowers are your best clues.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its rattlesnake root relatives, three-leaved rattlesnake root is distinguished by its trifoliate leaves - most others have simple, undivided leaves.
Tall rattlesnake root lives up to its name by being the tallest of the New England rattlesnake roots, often reaching 6 feet compared to the 2-3 foot height of white rattlesnake root.
Alpine rattlesnake root is much smaller and more delicate than its lowland cousins like tall rattlesnake root, and its flowers are distinctly pale yellow rather than purple or white.
Among New England's rattlesnake roots, white rattlesnake root has the smallest flower heads and the most variable leaf shapes.

Lion's foot rattlesnake root stands out from its rattlesnake root relatives by having the most dramatically lobed leaves - they're much more deeply cut than white rattlesnake root's triangular leaves or tall rattlesnake root's broader, less-divided foliage.
